item.title: Corporate America Needs a Spine, Not a New Weathervane
item.description: The Vicar of Bray is an 18th-century song with a catchy tune and a highly relevant message. The song traces the contortions of a place-hunting clergyman as the ideological winds change direction. He is a Roman Catholic under James II, a Tory under Queen Anne and a Whig under George I.
item.dc:creator: Adrian Wooldridge

item.title: Flock: Police Enforcement Cameras Can Do a Lot of Good
item.description: The first license-plate-reading cameras in the US were installed 40 years ago in Galveston County, Texas. They were supposed to catch speeders, but Texas law didn’t really provide for a means of enforcement and almost everybody hated them. Within a year or so they were gone.
item.dc:creator: Justin Fox

item.title: Driving Away International Students Will Cost the US
item.description: As Democrats lay out their priorities for wielding power in Congress, they’ve been right to put a renewed focus on President Donald Trump’s hardline immigration agenda, given the disastrous effects it has had on Americans’ lives and livelihoods. They just shouldn’t forget what it’s doing to higher education too.
item.dc:creator: Erika D. Smith

item.title: Nvidia Interim CEO Colette Kress and the Glass Cliff After Huang
item.description: If part one of the Nvidia Corp. saga centered on the fall of one of the world’s wealthiest and most powerful men, then part two is turning into an all-too-familiar tale about the impossible expectations placed on the woman asked to pick up the pieces.
item.dc:creator: Beth Kowitt

item.title: Fix the Electoral College, But Not With the National Popular Vote Compact
item.description: The Electoral College is a relic of a time when state legislatures, not voters, picked presidential candidates. And the proposed National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, gaining momentum after the Democrats won control of several state governments in this month’s elections, is a clever idea about how to change it.
item.dc:creator: Noah Feldman

item.title: Amazon’s Standard-Bearer Act on Climate Is Wearing Thin
item.description: Meeting publicly announced goals is tricky, but it gets much easier when you set the key performance indicator as “Trust me, bro.”
item.dc:creator: Mark Gongloff

item.title: Measles Returns: RFK Jr. and US Health Officials Are Dropping the Ball
item.description: Six decades after the US found a safe, effective and affordable way to prevent measles deaths, the disease is back. On Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning the virus had been circulating uninterrupted for at least a year.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Trump's Corruption Problem Won't Disappear With Susie Wiles
item.description: Americans have loudly proclaimed they’re fed up with government corruption. The problem for both Democrats and Republicans is that while President Donald Trump has used government to enrich himself, not all the corruption oozing from Washington emanates from him. For decades, a revolving door of government insiders and K Street lobbying firms from both parties has normalized an industry that profits off government connections and pay-to-play politics. Trump has just supercharged it.
item.dc:creator: Mary Ellen Klas

item.dc:creator: Dave Lee

item.title: Federal Reserve Should Avoid Aggressive Rate Hikes in This Economy
item.description: Americans are justifiably losing patience after six years of elevated inflation rates. So, too, are some key central bankers. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller, an influential voter on monetary policy who contended with Chair Kevin Warsh for the top job earlier in the year, said this week that he was prepared to “shock people” by raising interest rates by half a percentage point when policymakers meet in three weeks to help contain inflation. item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: UK-EU Summit: Britain's Big EU Summit Could've Been an Email
item.description: The most notable thing about Friday’s UK-EU summit, where British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet the leaders of the European Union in Brussels, is that it needs to happen at all. The agreements likely to be announced — on food and agricultural trade and carbon-trading schemes — are hardly of earth-shattering consequence to the EU’s technocrats. For them, this meeting could have been an email.
item.dc:creator: Mihir Sharma

item.title: Italian Ski Slopes Really Do Not Need a KFC at The Top
item.description: Italy’s Dolomites are in the midst of a tourism boom, and there is nothing wrong with that. Still, opening a Kentucky Fried Chicken at the top of a ski slope in Cortina d’Ampezzo — co-host of the 2026 Winter Olympics — is an insult to mountain lovers like me. And my 12-year-old son agrees, so this isn’t just a middle-aged lament about unwanted change.
item.dc:creator: Tommaso Ebhardt

item.title: Beauty Advent Calendars Are a Holiday Gift to Makeup Brands
item.description: If you are lucky enough to open the door of an advent calendar on Dec. 1, you are part of a global retail phenomenon.
